Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 65
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Military Medic
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Car Similarity: Similar cars
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress, Distraction: I distract myself with something else, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

Vignette:
Alice is a 65-year-old woman who lives alone in a small apartment on the outskirts of a Midwestern city. She was a military medic for over thirty years, retiring just three years ago. Her husband of forty years died two years before her retirement, and since then she has lived quietly, keeping mostly to herself. She came to therapy at the urging of her daughter, who had grown concerned about the weight Alice had gained, the way she had stopped driving, and how she no longer visited her grandchildren.

The event that changed everything happened eighteen months ago, on a rainy November evening. Alice was driving home from the grocery store when a car ran a red light and T-boned her vehicle at an intersection. She remembers the sound—a violent, metallic crunch that seemed to come from inside her own chest—and the way her body jerked against the seatbelt. She was not badly injured physically, but she remembers the moment of impact with a clarity that feels like a curse. In the seconds afterward, she sat in the driver's seat, unable to move, her hands frozen on the wheel, while a young man from the other car screamed for help. She was a medic, trained for this, but she could not make her legs work. She could not get out of the car. She sat there, heart pounding, until the paramedics arrived and pried her door open.

Since that night, Alice has not been the same. She cannot drive past that intersection, and eventually she stopped driving altogether. She gave her car to her son-in-law and now relies on buses or her daughter for rides, but even being a passenger is difficult. When she sees a car that looks like the one that hit her—a dark blue sedan, same make and model—her stomach drops and she feels a rush of heat, as if she is back in that driver's seat. She has become hypervigilant to the point of exhaustion. Every unexpected sound—a truck backfiring, a door slamming, a child dropping a heavy toy—makes her flinch and scan the room for an exit. Her body is constantly tense; she describes it as "waiting for the next thing to hit." She wakes up with her jaw clenched and her shoulders tight, and she goes to bed the same way.

The memory of the crash comes to her not as a story she tells, but as a reliving. When she thinks about it, she feels the impact again, smells the wet asphalt, hears the screaming. She knows what happened—she can describe the sequence of events—but when the memory surges, words fail her. She becomes so overwhelmed by emotion that she has to stop whatever she is doing and sit down until the feeling passes. Sometimes she feels as if she is actually back in the car, her hands gripping an invisible steering wheel, her body braced for a collision that has already happened.

To manage this, Alice has developed habits that she knows are not healthy but that feel necessary. She tries hard not to think about the trauma at all. When a related thought surfaces, she pushes it away, sometimes physically shaking her head as if to dislodge it. She distracts herself constantly—television shows she does not really watch, crossword puzzles she cannot finish, long walks that she takes only on quiet streets. And she eats. She eats more than she ever has before, especially in the evenings when the house is quiet and her mind has fewer distractions. She tells herself it is just comfort, but she knows, somewhere underneath, that the fullness in her stomach helps her feel something other than the dread that lives just beneath her skin.

The consequences are visible. She has gained nearly forty pounds in a year, and her doctor has warned her about her blood pressure. She has stopped attending her weekly bridge group because one of the members drives a dark blue sedan. She no longer visits her grandchildren because the drive to their house involves crossing that intersection. Her daughter has noticed, and her worry is what finally brought Alice to the clinic. Alice came because she is afraid of her own life shrinking further. She is afraid that she will never feel safe again, and she is desperate to find a way to live without being haunted by a single moment she cannot escape.
